newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya, Rwanda recognise change in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Kenya, Rwanda recognise change in Zaire.

text.p: Kenya and Rwanda said on Sunday they recognised the government to be formed in Zaire by Laurent Kabila, whose Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo has proclaimed victory in the civil war.
"Rwandans are very pleased," said Emmanuel Ndahiro, a senior adviser to Vice-President and Defence Minister Paul Kagame.
"Mobutu (Sese Seko) has finally gone. We think that is an achievement not only for Zaireans but also for African resolve," Ndahiro told Reuters in Nairobi by telephone from Kigali.

In Nairobi, Kenyan Foreign Minister Kalonzo Musyoka said: "In keeping with our traditions, we work with governments that are in place. The government Kabila will be forming will be an important development in the sub-region and I can without hesitation say that we shall work with it."
"It was thought that Kenya may have been anti-Kabila. No, we were not. Kenya has always been pro the people of Zaire and pro the plight of the suffering," he told a news conference.
"Events within the past seven months in Zaire pointed at a revolution led by the people themselves," Musyoka added.

Last year and early this year, Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi convened regional summits on the Zaire crisis but did not invite Kabila to either. Kabila also said at the time he would not like to visit Nairobi because he saw Moi as being too close to ousted president Mobutu Sese Seko.
Musyoka said that Kabila was excluded from the Nairobi talks because he was not a member of any government at the time and rules of diplomacy made direct contact with Kabila difficult.

He added: "We are pleased that at least as of now, the unity of Zaire seems to be guaranteed. Kenya has always maintained a policy of positive neutrality with regard to the conflict. We have operated above board with a clear concept of clean hands."

Last week, Moi and Kabila spoke for the first time since Kabila launched his rebellion in October last year. The talks took place after Kabila met Moi's special envoy, Lonrho East Africa Chairman Mark Too, in Lubumbashi.

Mobutu accused Rwandan troops of fighting alongside Kabila. Ndahiro said: "Whether or not we provided troops is no longer an issue. Mobutu and his forces have been defeated by whatever composition of Kabila's soldiers. That is the point."
In Dar es Salaam on Saturday, Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa said Tanzania would work with any government formed by Kabila and he had no objection to dealing with Kabila.

Earlier, the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) acknowledged the civil war triumph of Kabila and his rebels and called for a broad-based transitional authority representing Zaireans of other political shades.
"Mr Kabila and the AFDL have won the civil war and the challenge before them now is to win and consolidate the peace," said OAU Secretary-General Salim Ahmed Salim.
There was no immediate government reaction from Uganda, considered one of Kabila's closest allies.
